coaching.title: Opening the game
coaching.body:
At the start of a hand, your first play has to be either a double or a scoring tile. A strong strategy is to look for a double that keeps your turn going but leaves you with no legal follow up play.

For example, if you play the double-1 and you do not have any other 1s in your hand, your turn continues because doubles keep you playing. But since you now have no playable tile, the game forces you to draw.

That might sound bad at first, but in Racehorse, more tiles can mean more power. Drawing gives you more options, more scoring chances, and more ways to control the hand later.

coaching.title: Take the First Scoring 1
coaching.body:
After drawing, this was the first playable 1 we found, and it immediately turns the open count from 2 to 5. Since 5 is a scoring number, this play scores 1 point and keeps our turn alive.

For a beginner, the key idea is simple: when the game gives you a scoring play, especially after a forced draw, you usually take it. Scoring does not just add points — it also lets you keep control of the turn and look for the next play.

coaching.title: Choose the Safer 3 to Limit the Counterplay
coaching.body:
Even when two tiles both fit, the best move is not always the one that looks most natural. Here, 3-2 is better than 3-4 because 3-4 would give the opponent a dangerous reply with the double-4, creating an easy scoring chance.

By playing 3-2, you avoid setting up that opportunity and make the next turn less favorable for your opponent. This is a key beginner lesson: do not only ask, “What can I play?” Also ask, “What does this let my opponent play next?”

coaching.title: Save Your 5s for Better Scoring Chances
coaching.body:
This is a low-option position, so the goal is not to make a fancy move — it is to avoid wasting your best scoring tiles too early. Playing 2-0 on the right keeps the hand moving without spending a 5, which can be much more valuable later when it can turn the open count into a multiple of five.

In Racehorse, 5s are often power tiles because they create scoring opportunities and can keep your turn alive. If a non-scoring tile gets the job done, it is usually better to save your 5s for a spot where they actually score or extend a chain.

coaching.title: Cash In the Double-6
coaching.body:
This is a scoring setup, and the double-6 is the tile that turns it into points. By playing it here, the open count moves from 19 to 25, which is a multiple of five, so you score 5 points and your turn continues.

The important beginner lesson is that doubles are not only for extending your turn — they can also be major scoring weapons when the open count is already close to a multiple of five. Here, the double-6 is not just playable; it is the tile that converts the position into a scoring chain.

coaching.title: Keep the Open Ends on a Multiple of 5
coaching.body:
After scoring with the double-6, the best follow-up is to keep the scoring chain going. Playing 5-0 off the 5 changes the open count from 25 to 20, which is still a multiple of five. That means you score again — 4 more points — and your turn continues.

This is a core Racehorse concept: once you are in a scoring chain, look for moves that preserve the count on a multiple of 5. You are not just making a legal play — you are protecting the scoring setup and squeezing more value out of the same turn.

coaching.title: End the Turn Without Opening Extra Branches
coaching.body:
Here, 2-5 on the left is the cleanest way to finish the chain. The key reason is board control: you do not have blanks, so you do not want to play across the double-6 or double-3 and create extra open lanes you may not be able to use.

Opening more branches can help your opponent more than it helps you, especially when your hand is not built to take advantage of them. By playing 2-5 on the left, you make your move, end the turn, and avoid giving the board more flexibility than necessary.

coaching.title: Reduce the Playable Lanes
coaching.body:
There is not a big scoring opportunity here, so the goal is board control. Playing 5-6 turns the open 5 into a 6, which lowers the number of easy playable lines available after your move.

This kind of move is not about scoring right away. It is about making the board a little harder for your opponent to use. When you cannot score, look for the play that leaves behind the least helpful board.

coaching.title: Score With 4-6 to Keep the Turn Alive
coaching.body:
Here, 4-6 is the scoring move. It changes the open count from 18 to 20, which is a multiple of five, so you score 4 points and your turn continues.

That continuation matters because after taking the points, you still have the chance to finish the hand on your next play.

coaching.title: Go Out and Collect the Opponent’s Pips
coaching.body:
After scoring with 4-6, your turn continues, and now you can go out cleanly with 3-4. Going out ends the hand, and then you collect points from the pips left in your opponent’s hand.

Those leftover pips are added up and converted into points. For example, if your opponent is left with 4-5, 5-5, and 2-1, that is 22 total pips. In Racehorse scoring, that would be worth 4 points. If they had 23 pips, it would round up to 5 points.

coaching.title: Start Thinking One Move Ahead
coaching.body:
Here, the move is not just about playing the double-3 by itself. The real idea is seeing the chain before you start it.

Playing the double-3 keeps your turn alive because doubles let you continue. From there, you can follow up with 0-4 on the left, which brings the open count to 10 and scores 2 points.

This is where Racehorse starts to become more than just matching tiles. You are not only asking, “What can I play right now?” You are asking, “What does this move let me play next?”

coaching.title: Finish the Chain With the Scoring 0-4
coaching.body: This is the follow-up we were setting up. After playing the double-3, the turn continues, and now 0-4 is the tile that turns the open count from 6 to 10. Since 10 is a multiple of five, this scores 2 points and keeps the turn alive.

coaching.title: Dump a Double When Your Hand Is Double-Heavy
coaching.body:
After the scoring play, this is a good time to start getting rid of the double-4. This hand has a lot of doubles, which can be awkward because doubles are only strong when you have follow-up tiles to support them.

If you are holding too many doubles without enough matching tiles, they can become hard to use later. Playing the double-4 here keeps your turn alive and starts clearing one of those risky tiles out of your hand.

coaching.title: Play the Only Follow-Up
coaching.body:
After playing the double-4, your turn continues because doubles keep you playing. From there, 0-3 is the only follow-up available, so this move is about completing the chain as cleanly as possible.

Not every continuation is a big scoring setup. Sometimes the right move is simply to recognize that your double gave you one extra play, then take the only legal tile and keep the hand moving.

coaching.title: Dump the Doubles While the Board Allows It
coaching.body:
This is the start of a double-dump chain. You still have multiple doubles left, and right now the open ends line up with them, so this is a good chance to start clearing them out.

Playing the double-2 keeps your turn alive and removes one of the risky doubles from your hand. When your hand has too many doubles, you do not want to wait too long — if the matching ends disappear, those doubles can get stuck.

coaching.title: Keep Dumping the Doubles
coaching.body:
Since another open end matches your double-5, you can dump that next and continue the chain. 

The key idea is not that the double-5 has to be second every time. The important part is recognizing that you have a rare window where multiple doubles are all playable, so you should use that window before the board changes.

coaching.title: Clear the Last Double
coaching.body:
Now you can finish the double dump by playing the double-0. This clears the last awkward double from your hand while the board still supports it.

The exact order is not always the main point. In live play, what matters is seeing that all three doubles have matching open ends and using the chain to unload them while you can.

coaching.title: Use the New Tile to Keep Scoring
coaching.body:
After dumping the last double, the hand is not over yet because you cannot finish on a double or a scoring continuation. Since the turn had to continue, you were dealt another tile — and the 4-6 is exactly what you want to see.

Now you can play 4-6 off the open 4 branch, which changes the open count from 14 to 20. Since 20 is a multiple of five, this scores 4 points and keeps your turn alive again.

coaching.title: Go Out With a Clean Final Tile
coaching.body:
After scoring with 4-6, the turn continues and now 3-4 is the clean final play. It does not create a multiple of five, and it is not a double, so it can safely end the hand.

That matters because you cannot go out on a scoring play or a double. Here, 3-4 is exactly what you want: a normal legal tile that empties your hand and ends the round.

coaching.title: Force the Draw With Double-1
coaching.body:
Once again, at the start of the hand, you can open with a double or a scoring tile. Here, double-1 is a strong opener because it keeps your turn alive, but you do not have any other 1s to follow it with.

That means after playing the double, you are forced to draw. In Racehorse, that can actually be good because drawing gives you more tiles, more options, and more chances to build a scoring chain.

coaching.title: Going In Does Not Always Pay Off Immediately
coaching.body:
After forcing the draw, sometimes you will not get much. Here, 1-5 is basically all you have, so you just play it and move on. It does not score, and it does not continue the turn, but it is still the only real option.

That is part of the risk of going in. You are drawing for more power, but the payoff is not guaranteed every time. Some draws only give you a simple playable tile. Other times, though, going in gives you a huge advantage — more options, more scoring chances, and stronger chains that your opponent cannot match.

coaching.title: Take the 0-3 Score
coaching.body:
Here, 0-3 is the scoring move. It changes the open count from 2 to 5, which is a multiple of five, so you score 1 point and your turn continues.

This is a simple but important habit: whenever you have a playable tile, check whether it moves the open count onto a multiple of five. Even a small score matters because it keeps your turn alive and gives you another chance to build the hand.

coaching.title: Follow the Score With 3-4
coaching.body: No reason to dump the double-3 here, just play the 3-4 and limit your opponent's options.

coaching.title: Cut Down the Easy Numbers
coaching.body:
There is not a scoring chain here, so the goal is to leave the board a little less comfortable for the opponent. Playing 4-6 off the open 6 changes the open count from 14 to 12 and reduces some of the easier scoring pressure on the board.

This kind of move is about damage control. When you cannot score or continue, try to play the tile that leaves behind fewer useful options instead of opening the board up for your opponent.

coaching.title: Only one choice
coaching.body: Here, there is not much to decide. 2-4 is the only playable tile, so you take it and keep the hand moving.

coaching.title: Take the Points and Go In
coaching.body:
Here, 5-6 is the scoring move. Playing it off the double-6 drops the open count from 17 to 10, which scores 2 points and keeps your turn alive.

But after that, you do not have any 5s, 6s, 0s, or 1s to follow up with, so this scoring play also sends you in (the boneyard). That means you take the points first, then the game forces you to draw because your turn is still active and you have no playable tile.

coaching.title: Boneyard reward
coaching.body: After going in, you pull the double-5 from the boneyard, one of the best tiles you can draw. Since your turn is still alive, you can stack it onto the open 5 for more points and keep the chain going.

coaching.title: Cut the Count Down With 5-3
coaching.body: After stacking the double-5, your turn continues, but there is no score available here. So the best move is to play 5-3 off the double and cut the open count down from 15 to 8.

coaching.title: Take the Risk When Your Hand Can Support It
coaching.body: Here, I chose to play 2-6 off the open 6 because we still have other 6s in the hand, and the other options do not feel as strong. This move changes the board in a way that may make things harder for the opponent, possibly even sending them into the boneyard.

coaching.title: Count the Dead Numbers and Save Your 6s
coaching.body:
This is where you start thinking beyond just the tile in your hand. The opponent has already played through the remaining 6s, and you can see that five 6s are already on the board. Since there are only seven of each number, and you still have two 6s in your hand, that means you are holding the last two.

That makes your 6s valuable. Instead of spending one now, you play off the 3 with 1-3 and save the 6s for later. When you know a number is almost gone, holding the last ones can give you control because your opponent is less likely to be able to answer that number.

coaching.title: Dump the Double-4 While It Is Playable
coaching.body:
Here, double-4 is a good dump. It does not score, but it keeps your turn alive and gets rid of a double while the board still gives you a clean place to play it.

This is important because doubles can become awkward if you hold them too long. They are powerful when you can use them, but if the matching number disappears, they can get stuck in your hand.

coaching.title: Follow the Double With 4-6
coaching.body:
After the double-4, your turn continues, so now you follow with 4-6. This uses the extra play from the double and brings the open count from 8 to 6.

It does not score, but it does clean up another tile and leaves you with fewer awkward pieces. That is still useful — not every chain has to score. Sometimes the value is in dumping a double, using the forced continuation, and improving your hand.

coaching.title: Opening a New Branch
coaching.body:
Here, I played 5-6 by creating a new line, but looking back, this is a move I would probably take back. I was worried that if I played 3-2, the opponent might answer with the double-2 and score, so I tried to avoid giving them that setup.

The problem is that creating a new branch can also help the opponent. It opens the board up, increases the number of playable lanes, and gives them more ways to respond. In hindsight, the better idea would be to play in a way that keeps the board tighter instead of adding more options.

coaching.title: Take the 3-2 Score
coaching.body: Now 3-2 becomes the scoring move. Playing it off the open 3 brings the open count from 11 to 10, which is a multiple of five, so you score 2 points and your turn continues.

coaching.title: Play the Only Follow-Up After the Draw
coaching.body: After scoring with 3-2, the turn continues, but there is no immediate follow-up in hand, so you have to draw. Once you pick up 0-2, that becomes the only playable tile, so you play it.

coaching.title: Start the hand With Double-2
coaching.body:
To start this hand, you do not have a clean way to force a draw, so the next best idea is to look for a scoring chain. The double-2 is the starter because doubles keep your turn alive, which gives you a chance to follow up with another tile.

This move does not score by itself, but it sets up the next play. That is the key: sometimes the first tile in a chain is not the payoff — it is the tile that keeps your turn going long enough to reach the payoff.

coaching.title: Choose the Higher-Scoring Follow-Up
coaching.body:
After the double-2, you have more than one scoring follow-up. Both 2-1 and 2-6 can work, but 2-6 is the better choice because it scores more.

That is an important beginner habit: when multiple plays score, do not just take the first one you see. Compare them and choose the one that gives you the most points while still keeping your hand playable.

coaching.title: Cross the Double-2 With Your Only Move
coaching.body:
After the scoring follow-up, your turn continues, and 2-1 is the only move available. Since it plays off the double-2, this move crosses the double and opens the double’s branches.

That means the double is no longer just one straight path — it now creates additional playable lanes from that double. Opening branches can give both players more options, so normally you want to be careful with it. But here, there is no real choice: 2-1 is the only playable tile, so you take the move and deal with the new board afterward.

coaching.title: Use the Simple 0-4
coaching.body: Here, there is no score to chase, so 0-4 is just the practical move. It gets a tile out of your hand and keeps you from forcing something that is not there.

coaching.title: Dump the Double-4 When You Can
coaching.body: The double-4 does not score here, but it keeps your turn alive and clears a double from your hand. That still has value, especially because doubles can become awkward if you hold them too long.

coaching.title: Follow With the Only Useful Play
coaching.body:
After the double keeps your turn going, 0-5 is the follow-up. It does not score, but it uses the extra play and keeps reducing your hand.

This is a normal part of Racehorse: sometimes a chain is not about points, it is just about using the continuation to clean up.

coaching.title: Clear the Double-0
coaching.body: The double-0 is another dump. It does not change the open count much, but it keeps the turn alive and removes your last awkward double from the hand.

coaching.title: Finish With the Only Tile Left
coaching.body: After the double-0, your turn continues, and 0-6 is the tile you have to play. It does not score, but it empties your hand and ends the hand cleanly because it is not a double and does not make the open count a multiple of five.

coaching.title: Make the Clean 1-4 Play
coaching.body: Here, 1-4 does not score or continue the turn, but it is a clean playable tile that keeps the hand moving. Sometimes there is no big chain to build, so the goal is simply to make the best available move without overcomplicating it.

coaching.title: Play 0-5 to Cut the Count Down
coaching.body: Here, 0-5 is mainly a board-control move. It drops the open count from 13 to 3, which makes the board less immediately dangerous and avoids leaving the count close to a scoring number.

coaching.title: Use 1-2 as the Available Move
coaching.body: This is another simple turn where 1-2 is the move available. It does not score, but it gets a tile out of your hand and changes the board from 2 to 1

coaching.title: Dump the Double-1
coaching.body: Here, double-1 is useful because it clears a double from your hand and keeps your turn alive. Even though it does not score, doubles can become hard to get rid of later, so playing one when it fits is usually valuable.

coaching.title: Follow the Double With a Score
coaching.body: After the double-1, your turn continues, and now 3-6 turns the open count from 8 to 5. Since 5 is a scoring number, you score 1 point and keep the turn alive again.

coaching.title: Keep the Chain Alive With Double-3
coaching.body: After scoring, the turn continues again, and double-3 lets you keep the chain going. It does not score, but it clears another double and gives you one more chance to play

coaching.title: Finish the Chain With 5-6
coaching.body: After the double-3, you follow with 5-6. It does not score, but it uses the continuation and is the only move we have

coaching.title: Play the Simple 0-2
coaching.body: Here, 0-2 is just the clean available move.Sometimes you just make the legal move, reduce your hand, and wait for a better scoring chance later.

coaching.title: Follow With the 0-3
coaching.body: 0-3 is our only choice here

coaching.title: Open With the 4-6 Score
coaching.body: To start this hand, 4-6 is the scoring opener. It brings the open count from 0 to 10, which scores 2 points and keeps your turn alive.

coaching.title: Keep the Chain Going With 6-1
coaching.body:
After the opening score, your turn continues, and 6-1 is the next scoring move. It changes the open count from 10 to 5, which scores 1 more point and keeps your turn alive again.

This is exactly what you want from a scoring chain: one score creates the next chance, and you keep squeezing value out of the same turn.

coaching.title: Finish the Chain With 2-4
coaching.body: After scoring twice, 2-4 is the follow-up that finishes the chain. It does not score, but it uses the continuation you earned and gets another tile out of your hand.

coaching.title: Play the 0-3
coaching.body: Here, 0-3 is a better move than 0-5. It does not score, but it keeps the hand moving and gets one tile out and saves the 5's for scoring

coaching.title: Use 3-5 to Keep Moving
coaching.body: The 3-5 does not score here, but it is a playable tile that continues reducing your hand. Sometimes the right move is just the one that gets you closer to a cleaner finish.

coaching.title: Play 3-6 and Change the Board
coaching.body: Here, 3-6 changes the board without scoring. It is not a big payoff move, but it moves you off the current open number and leaves a new shape for the next turn.

coaching.title: Take the Simple 0-5
coaching.body: Only move available. It does not score, but it uses the open blank and keeps your hand moving forward.

coaching.title: Find the Small Score With 2-5
coaching.body: Here, 2-5 brings the open count from 8 to 5, which scores 1 point and keeps your turn alive. It is only a small score, but the continuation is valuable.

coaching.title: Use the Extra Turn With 2-3
coaching.body: After scoring, your turn continues, and 2-3 is the follow-up. We did not get a tile to go out cleanly with, so now the round continues.

coaching.title: Finish Cleanly With 4-5
coaching.body: Here, 4-5 is the final play. It does not score and it is not a double, so it can cleanly end the hand.

coaching.title: Start the Chain With 2-5
coaching.body:
Here, 2-5 is the first scoring move. It brings the open count from 9 to 10, which scores 2 points and keeps your turn alive.

This is the move that starts the chain. Once you see a scoring tile, take the points first, then look for how the continuation lets you keep building.

coaching.title: Keep Scoring With 5-0
coaching.body:
After the first score, your turn continues, and 5-0 is the next scoring play. It changes the open count from 10 to 5, which scores 1 more point and keeps the chain alive again.

This is a strong habit to build: after every score, immediately re-check the open count and see if you can score again.

coaching.title: Use the Double-0 to Extend the Turn
coaching.body:
After scoring again, double-0 is a good way to keep the chain going. It scores another 1 point here and, because it is a double, your turn continues.

Double blanks can be valuable because they let you extend a chain without adding much to the board. Here, it gives you another playable step and keeps control of the turn.

coaching.title: Finish the Chain With 2-4
coaching.body:
After the double-0, the turn continues, and 2-4 is the follow-up that ends the chain. It does not score, but it uses the extra play you earned and gets another tile out of your hand.

This is a clean way to finish a productive turn: score, score again, extend with the double, then use the final continuation to reduce your hand.

coaching.title: Play 4-6 to Keep the Hand Moving
coaching.body: Here, 4-6 does not score, but it is a clean playable tile that gets one out of your hand. When there is no scoring chain available, the goal is to keep moving and avoid forcing a bad setup.

coaching.title: Dump the Double-6
coaching.body:
Now you can play the double-6. It does not score here, but it keeps your turn alive and gets a dangerous double out of your hand.

Doubles are powerful, but they can also trap you if the board changes and you lose access to that number.

coaching.title: Use the Double’s Extra Turn
coaching.body:
After the double-6, your turn continues, so you follow with 5-6. This does not score, but it uses the continuation and gets another tile out of your hand.

This is still a productive chain: you dumped a double and used the extra play to reduce your hand further.

coaching.title: Find the Big 1-3 Score
coaching.body:
Here, 1-3 is a big scoring move. It changes the open count from 27 to 25, which scores 5 points and keeps your turn alive.

This is a great example of why you always check the count before playing. A small-looking tile can be worth a lot when it lands the board on a multiple of five.

coaching.title: Finish Cleanly With 1-4
coaching.body:
After scoring, your turn continues, and 1-4 lets you go out cleanly. It does not score and it is not a double, so it can end the hand.

That is exactly what you want after a scoring play: take the points first, then finish with a normal tile that does not force another continuation.

coaching.title: Take the Points, Then Look for Control
coaching.body: Here, 4-6 is a strong opener because it immediately scores 2 points and keeps your turn alive.

coaching.title: Play What the Hand Gives You
coaching.body: After the opening score, the next move is not a big setup, you are mostly playing what you have. Sometimes after scoring, the follow-up is just about using the continuation and keeping your hand moving.

coaching.title: Keep the Hand Moving With the Next Legal Tile
coaching.body:
This is another simple move where you are mostly following the board. There is no major scoring moment here, but you are still reducing your hand and keeping yourself in position for the next turn.

A lot of strong Racehorse play is patience. You take the points when they are there, and when they are not, you avoid forcing bad moves.

coaching.title: Score Off the Branch With 3-6
coaching.body:
Now the scoring chance appears. Playing 3-6 off the branch brings the open count to a multiple of five, so you take the points and keep your turn alive.

This is why branches matter. They create extra open ends, and if you are paying attention, one of those branches can become the scoring lane.

coaching.title: Force the Board Onto One Number
coaching.body:
After the board develops, the key idea is control. By using your final 2, you force the board into a position where the open ends are basically all 2s.

That is powerful because there are only seven tiles of each number. If most of the 2s are already accounted for, then forcing the board onto 2s can trap the opponent.

coaching.title: Trap Fritz and Win on Pips
coaching.body:
Once the board is locked on 2s, Fritz is forced into the boneyard. Since the remaining playable 2s are either already gone, in your control, or locked in the final boneyard tiles, Fritz gets stuck after drawing.

That means the hand ends with Fritz holding a lot of pips, and you collect those points. This is a perfect example of winning without simply going out — you controlled the board, trapped the opponent, and used their remaining hand to push yourself over the target score.
